entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To fail or turn out badly in a very serious, often shocking way.
entries.usage: Common in news, stories and conversation, especially about plans, operations and events that end in disaster: *The robbery went horribly wrong*. *Something went horribly wrong* is a frequent fixed sentence, and *terribly* or *badly* can replace *horribly*. The subject is a plan, event or process, not a person.
examples: Our attempt at a homemade wedding cake **went horribly wrong**: it collapsed an hour before the reception.
Police say the robbery **went horribly wrong** when the store owner fought back.
A routine software update **went horribly wrong** and grounded thousands of flights.

drill.sentence: The camping trip {{went horribly wrong}} when a storm flooded our tent at two in the morning.
drill.hint: failed in a very bad way (adverb: not *terribly* or *badly*)

entries.related: *go south* — informal, start to fail; *backfire* — have the opposite effect of what was intended; *go off without a hitch* — happen perfectly, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To waste a good chance through carelessness, poor decisions or lack of effort.
entries.usage: Common in sports reporting, politics, business and personal advice; it sounds critical and a little formal. Typical objects are *an opportunity*, *a chance*, *a lead*, *a fortune* and *talent*. In sports, a team that *squanders a lead* loses a winning position.
entries.pattern: squander an opportunity / a chance / a lead
examples: He was offered a full scholarship but **squandered the opportunity** by skipping most of his classes.
The team **squandered** a golden **opportunity** to win the title, losing at home to the worst team in the league.
Critics say the city **squandered an opportunity** to build affordable housing when land was still cheap.

drill.sentence: Don't {{squander this opportunity}}; most people never get the chance to study abroad for free.
drill.hint: carelessly throw away (verb: not *waste*, *miss* or *blow*)

entries.related: *miss an opportunity* — fail to use a chance, without the idea of carelessness; *seize an opportunity* — the opposite; *fritter away* — waste money or time slowly on small things.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To suffer serious consequences or lose a lot because of something you did or failed to do.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and storytelling, often as a warning: *You'll pay dearly for this*. The pattern is *pay dearly for* + mistake or action, or *pay dearly* alone at the end of a sentence. It usually refers to suffering or loss rather than money, although it can also mean paying a very high price.
examples: I skipped stretching before the race, and I **paid dearly for** it the next day.
The team **paid dearly for** its defensive mistakes in the second half.
The restaurant **paid dearly for** cutting corners on hygiene: after one bad inspection, the customers never came back.

drill.sentence: He ignored the doctor's advice for years and {{paid dearly for}} it with a heart attack at fifty.
drill.hint: suffered badly because of (verb + adverb; not *the price*)

entries.related: *pay the price for* — the same, less dramatic; *come back to bite you* — informal, a past mistake causes problems later; *get away with* — not suffer for a wrong, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To cause change to happen, especially social, political or organizational change.
entries.usage: Formal and common in politics, activism, nonprofits and leadership talk, often with *real*, *lasting* or *meaningful* before *change*. Here *effect* is a verb meaning *bring about*. In everyday speech, *make a difference* or *bring about change* sounds more natural.
examples: She ran for city council because she believed she could **effect change** from the inside.
A small group of nurses **effected** lasting **change** in how the hospital prevents patient falls.
A new CEO alone can't **effect change**; the whole company has to buy in.

drill.sentence: Complaining in the group chat rarely {{effects change}}; showing up at a town hall meeting often does.
drill.hint: brings about something new (formal verb + noun)

mistake.wrong: We want to affect change in our schools.
mistake.right: We want to effect change in our schools.
mistake.why: To *bring about* change, the verb is *effect*; *affect change* is a common error, even among native writers.

entries.related: *bring about change* — the same, less formal; *make a difference* — have a good effect, conversational; *drive change* — business jargon for pushing change forward.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To deal with a problem directly and immediately, instead of avoiding or delaying it.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics, sports and self-help: *We need to tackle this head-on*. *Head-on* comes after the object (*tackle the problem head-on*), and *deal with*, *face* and *address* also take it. It suggests courage and honesty, so leaders use it to show they are not hiding anything.
examples: Instead of hoping the rumors would die down, the principal **tackled** them **head-on** at a parents' meeting.
The new CEO promised to **tackle** the company's debt problem **head-on**.
If something bothers you about your roommate, it's better to **tackle** it **head-on** than let it build up.

drill.sentence: My mom never avoided hard conversations; she {{tackled them head-on}}, even when it was uncomfortable.
drill.hint: handled them directly and at once (verb: not *faced*, *addressed* or *dealt with*)

entries.related: *confront* — face a problem or person directly, often more aggressively; *sweep something under the rug* — hide a problem, the opposite; *take the bull by the horns* — deal boldly with a difficult situation.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To stop improving or growing after a period of steady progress.
entries.usage: Common in fitness, learning, careers, business and science: *My weight loss has hit a plateau*. *Reach a plateau* is a slightly more formal alternative. It usually describes a frustrating pause, and people often add *after* + time or *at* + level.
examples: I lost ten pounds in the first month, but then I **hit a plateau** and the scale wouldn't move.
Many language learners **hit a plateau** at the intermediate level.
Sales **hit a plateau** after the first year, so the company started looking for new markets.

drill.sentence: After a year of guitar lessons, I {{hit a plateau}} and couldn't seem to learn anything new.
drill.hint: stopped improving after steady progress (verb: not *reached*; noun: not *wall*)

entries.related: *hit a wall* — suddenly be unable to continue, often from exhaustion; *level off* — stop rising and stay steady, often about numbers; *stagnate* — fail to develop, more negative.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An arrangement you made earlier that prevents you from accepting a new invitation or request.
entries.usage: A polite, slightly formal way to decline, common in emails and replies to invitations: *Unfortunately, I have a prior commitment that evening*. It gives a reason without details, so people sometimes use it as a polite excuse. *A previous engagement* is more formal and a little old-fashioned.
entries.pattern: I have a prior commitment (that day / on + day)
examples: Thanks so much for the invitation, but I have **a prior commitment** on Saturday.
The CEO declined to speak at the conference, citing **a prior commitment**.
My daughter can't make the sleepover because she has **a prior commitment**: her grandma's birthday party.

drill.sentence: I'd love to help you move on Sunday, but I have {{a prior commitment}}, so how about Saturday?
drill.hint: something else already arranged (adjective: not *previous*; noun: not *engagement* or *conflict*)

entries.related: *a previous engagement* — the same, more formal; *have other plans* — casual and very common; *a scheduling conflict* — common at work, two events at the same time.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To reach the point where stress, pressure or a problem becomes too much and you can no longer cope or continue.
entries.usage: Used about people, relationships and systems such as hospitals or schools: *Nurses say they've reached a breaking point*. *Reach the breaking point* and *be at a breaking point* are common variants; British English often drops the article (*at breaking point*). It is frequent in news about strikes, health care and family stress.
entries.pattern: reach a / the breaking point; be at a breaking point
examples: After six months of night shifts with a newborn at home, she finally **reached a breaking point**.
Nurses say the understaffed emergency room has **reached a breaking point**.
Their arguments about money had **reached a breaking point**, and they started talking about divorce.

drill.sentence: After three weeks of drilling from the construction next door, I {{reached a breaking point}} and called the city.
drill.hint: got to the stage where I could no longer cope (not *the end of my rope*)

entries.related: *the last straw* — the final small problem that makes you lose control; *at the end of your rope* — informal, out of patience; *snap* — suddenly lose control.

entries.label: verb + adverb phrase
entries.meaning: To reject an idea, suggestion or claim immediately, without considering it seriously.
entries.usage: Common in discussions, debates, reviews and news, usually as a criticism or a warning: *Don't dismiss the idea out of hand*. *Out of hand* goes after the object, and *reject* also takes it. Don't confuse it with *get out of hand*, which means to become impossible to control.
entries.pattern: dismiss / reject + idea + out of hand
examples: My boss **dismissed** my idea **out of hand**, but two months later he presented it as his own.
Don't **dismiss** online therapy **out of hand**; it works well for a lot of people.
The landlord **dismissed** our request for new windows **out of hand**, calling it far too expensive.

drill.sentence: When I suggested selling the house, my dad didn't even think about it; he {{dismissed it out of hand}}.
drill.hint: turned it down at once, without thinking (verb: not *rejected*)

entries.related: *reject out of hand* — the same; *brush off* — informal, treat as unimportant; *give something a fair hearing* — consider it properly, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To change direction completely, especially to change a policy, decision or position to the opposite one.
entries.usage: Very common in American news about governments, companies, central banks and politicians: *The company reversed course after the backlash*. It is neutral, but it can suggest giving in to pressure. It often takes *on* + topic: *reverse course on tariffs*.
examples: After a wave of complaints, the airline **reversed course** and dropped the new bag fee.
My sister swore she'd never move back home, but after a year in the city she **reversed course**.
The central bank **reversed course** and started cutting interest rates.

drill.sentence: The school board planned to cut the music program, but after a flood of angry emails from parents, it {{reversed course}}.
drill.hint: switched to the opposite decision (not *backtracked* or *backed down*; verb: not *changed*)

entries.related: *backtrack* — withdraw from an earlier statement or plan; *do a U-turn* — change a policy completely, informal; *flip-flop* — critical, change positions again and again.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To develop, grow or move at the same speed as something else, so that you do not fall behind.
entries.usage: Very common in economics, technology, education and sports: *Wages haven't kept pace with inflation*. It is often negative: *fail to keep pace with*, *struggle to keep pace with*. *Keep up with* is the casual equivalent.
entries.pattern: keep pace with + change / demand / inflation
examples: Wages haven't **kept pace with** rising rents, so many families are struggling.
The runner **kept pace with** the leaders for twenty miles before dropping back.
Regulators are struggling to **keep pace with** advances in AI.

drill.sentence: The town's roads haven't {{kept pace with}} all the new housing, so rush hour is a nightmare now.
drill.hint: grown at the same rate as (not the casual phrasal verb with *up*)

entries.related: *keep up with* — casual, the same idea; *fall behind* — the opposite; *outpace* — move or grow faster than something.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A firm belief in the value of hard work, shown by working hard, reliably and responsibly.
entries.usage: Very common in American job ads, references, résumés and praise of people: *She has a strong work ethic*. The usual verb is *have*, and *great* or *incredible* can replace *strong* in speech. On a résumé it can sound like a cliché unless you back it up with examples.
examples: My grandfather worked two jobs until he was seventy; he had **a strong work ethic**.
Coaches love him because of his **strong work ethic**: he's always the first one at practice.
Many employers say **a strong work ethic** matters more to them than a perfect GPA.

drill.sentence: Our new babysitter is only sixteen, but she has {{a strong work ethic}}; she even folds the laundry without being asked.
drill.hint: a real commitment to effort and responsibility (adjective: not *good* or *great*)

mistake.wrong: He has a strong work ethics.
mistake.right: He has a strong work ethic.
mistake.why: *Work ethic* is singular; *ethics* means moral rules or their study, as in *medical ethics*.

entries.related: *diligent* — careful and hardworking, more formal; *a go-getter* — informal, an ambitious, energetic person; *a slacker* — informal, someone who avoids work.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To stay informed about the latest news or developments in a subject.
entries.usage: A little formal; common in job ads, professional emails and reports. The pattern is *keep / stay abreast of* + news, developments, changes or research. In conversation, *keep up with* or *stay on top of* is more natural.
entries.pattern: keep / stay abreast of + news / developments / changes
examples: I follow a few trade newsletters to **keep abreast of** what's happening in the industry.
Doctors must **keep abreast of** new treatments, so they take courses every year.
Our accountant **keeps abreast of** changes in the tax code, which saves us a lot of headaches.

drill.sentence: My grandmother is ninety, but she still watches the news every night to {{keep abreast of}} world events.
drill.hint: stay informed about (formal; the verb is not *stay*)

entries.related: *keep up with* — casual, the same idea; *stay on top of* — informal, follow closely and stay in control; *out of the loop* — not informed, the opposite.

entries.term: waste no time in doing something
entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To do something immediately and eagerly, without any delay.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports writing and storytelling, often with an admiring or slightly humorous tone: *She wasted no time in calling her lawyer*. It is usually in the past tense. *In* is often dropped, especially in speech: *He wasted no time getting started*.
examples: The new owners **wasted no time in** tearing down the old garage and building a pool.
After the coach was fired, rival teams **wasted no time in** contacting him.
My kids **wasted no time** opening their presents on Christmas morning.

drill.sentence: When the airfare dropped, my brother {{wasted no time in}} booking flights to Hawaii.
drill.hint: acted at once and eagerly (the verb is not *lost*)

entries.related: *lose no time in* — the same, more formal; *jump at the chance* — accept eagerly; *drag your feet* — delay on purpose, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To reach a point in a discussion or process where no progress is possible because the sides cannot agree.
entries.usage: Common in news about negotiations, politics, courts and labor disputes, and slightly formal. Typical subjects are *talks*, *negotiations* and *the two sides*; you can also *be at an impasse* or *break the impasse*. In conversation, *we're stuck* or *we've hit a dead end* is more natural.
entries.pattern: reach an impasse (over + issue); be at an impasse
examples: Budget negotiations in Congress have **reached an impasse**, raising fears of a government shutdown.
My brother and I **reached an impasse** about where to spend Thanksgiving, so Mom decided for us.
The neighbors **reached an impasse** over the shared fence and finally hired a mediator.

drill.sentence: The buyers wanted a lower price, the sellers wouldn't budge, and the negotiations {{reached an impasse}}.
drill.hint: got stuck with no progress possible (noun: not *deadlock* or *standstill*)

entries.related: *reach a deadlock* — the same, often about votes; *a stalemate* — neither side can win; *break the impasse* — find a way to move forward.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A person whom people tend either to support strongly or to oppose strongly, with few people in the middle.
entries.usage: Very common in American political and media commentary about politicians, celebrities, athletes and executives. It describes people's reaction rather than judging the person directly, so journalists use it to sound neutral. *Polarizing* also goes with *issue*, *topic* and *debate*.
examples: The coach is **a polarizing figure** among fans, and every loss reopens the debate about firing him.
As a talk-show host, she has become **a polarizing figure** in American media.
In our family, my outspoken uncle is a bit of **a polarizing figure** at Thanksgiving dinner.

drill.sentence: The chef is {{a polarizing figure}}: some diners call him a genius, and others say his food is all show.
drill.hint: a person who splits opinion sharply (adjective: not *divisive* or *controversial*)

entries.related: *a divisive figure* — very close, more critical; *a lightning rod* — a person who attracts criticism; *a unifying figure* — someone who brings people together, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To work very hard for a long time without stopping or losing energy, usually for a good cause.
entries.usage: Common in praise, speeches, news and thank-you messages: *Volunteers worked tirelessly to rebuild the school*. It is admiring and a little formal, and it often comes with *to* + verb or *for* + cause. In speeches and press releases it is so common that it can sound like a cliché.
entries.pattern: work tirelessly to + verb / for + cause
examples: Firefighters **worked tirelessly** through the night to keep the flames away from the houses.
My mother **worked tirelessly** to put all four of us through college.
The director thanked the crew, who had **worked tirelessly** for two years to finish the film.

drill.sentence: Our coach {{worked tirelessly}} to raise money for new uniforms, selling raffle tickets at every game.
drill.hint: put in huge effort without stopping (adverb: not *nonstop*)

entries.related: *work around the clock* — work day and night; *work your fingers to the bone* — informal, work extremely hard; *tireless* — the adjective, as in *a tireless advocate*.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To suddenly become too afraid to do something you had planned or started to do.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports and storytelling: *I was going to ask her out, but I lost my nerve*. It often comes with *at the last minute* or *at the last moment*. The opposite is *keep your nerve*, and *chicken out* is the informal equivalent.
entries.pattern: lose your nerve (at the last minute)
examples: I was going to tell my boss I was quitting, but I **lost my nerve** at the last minute.
The young golfer **lost his nerve** on the final hole and missed an easy putt.
When the market dropped, many investors **lost their nerve** and sold everything at a loss.

drill.sentence: She climbed all the way to the top of the high dive, then {{lost her nerve}} and climbed back down.
drill.hint: became too scared to go through with it (not *chickened out*)

mistake.wrong: When the kids kept screaming, I lost my nerves.
mistake.right: When the kids kept screaming, I lost my temper.
mistake.why: *Lose your nerve* (singular) means become too afraid to act; for getting angry, English says *lose your temper*.

entries.related: *chicken out* — informal, the same; *keep your nerve* — stay calm under pressure, the opposite; *get cold feet* — become nervous before a big commitment, like a wedding.

entries.term: summon the courage to do something
entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make yourself brave enough to do something difficult or frightening.
entries.usage: Common in storytelling and personal accounts, often about confessions, confrontations and big decisions. The pattern is *summon (up) the courage to* + verb, often with *finally* or *eventually*. *Muster (up) the courage* means the same.
examples: It took me three weeks to **summon the courage** to ask for a raise.
She finally **summoned the courage** to tell her parents she was dropping out of law school.
Years later, a former player **summoned the courage** to speak publicly about the abuse.

drill.sentence: I stood outside her door for ten minutes before I {{summoned the courage}} to knock and apologize.
drill.hint: made myself brave enough (verb: not *mustered*, *found* or *worked up*)

entries.related: *muster (up) the courage* — the same; *pluck up the courage* — the same, more British; *work up the nerve* — informal, build up courage slowly.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To speak openly and honestly, saying what you really think even if it is uncomfortable.
entries.usage: Common in interviews, journalism and meetings: *She spoke candidly about her struggles with depression*. It often comes with *about* + topic and suggests honesty about personal or sensitive matters. *Can I speak candidly?* is a polite way to warn that you are about to be very direct.
examples: In the interview, the actor **spoke candidly** about his years of addiction.
Can I **speak candidly**? I don't think this plan is going to work.
Doctors encourage patients to **speak candidly** about how much they drink.

drill.sentence: At the support group, people {{speak candidly}} about their grief, and nobody judges them.
drill.hint: talk with complete honesty (adverb: not *openly*, *frankly* or *freely*)

entries.related: *speak frankly* — very close, a bit more blunt; *off the record* — not to be quoted; *beat around the bush* — avoid saying something directly, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To destroy someone's hope that something good will happen, often suddenly.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and storytelling: *The injury dashed his hopes of a comeback*. It is often passive: *Her hopes were dashed*. The usual pattern is *dash someone's hopes of* + *-ing* or noun, or *for* + noun.
entries.pattern: dash someone's hopes (of + -ing / for + noun); hopes are dashed
examples: A knee injury **dashed her hopes** of making the Olympic team.
The bank's rejection letter **dashed our hopes** of buying a house this year.
Weeks of drought **dashed** the farmers' **hopes** for a good harvest.

drill.sentence: We had planned a beach weekend, but a forecast of storms on both days {{dashed our hopes}}.
drill.hint: suddenly ended what we were expecting (verb: not *crushed*)

entries.related: *crush someone's hopes* — similar, with stronger emotion; *raise someone's hopes* — make them hopeful, often unfairly; *pin your hopes on* — rely on something to succeed.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To rely on one particular person, plan or event to bring success or solve a problem.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and conversation, often with a hint that the hope is risky: *The team is pinning its hopes on a rookie quarterback*. The pattern is *pin your hopes on* + noun, and *all* can be added: *pin all your hopes on*. It is often in the continuous: *are pinning their hopes on*.
entries.pattern: pin (all) your hopes on + person / plan / event
examples: After two failed treatments, the family is **pinning their hopes on** a new clinical trial.
Don't **pin all your hopes on** one job interview; keep applying elsewhere.
The struggling mall is **pinning its hopes on** a new movie theater to bring shoppers back.

drill.sentence: My uncle is {{pinning his hopes on}} winning the lottery to pay for his retirement, which worries all of us.
drill.hint: relying completely on, for success (verb: not *banking* or *counting*)

entries.related: *bank on* — informal, depend on something happening; *put all your eggs in one basket* — risk everything on one plan; *dash someone's hopes* — destroy their hope.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Something that most people do not like at first but may learn to enjoy after trying it several times.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and reviews about food, drinks, music, art and humor: *Blue cheese is an acquired taste*. It is often a polite way to say that something is unusual or that you do not like it yet. About people it is humorous: *My uncle is an acquired taste*.
examples: Black coffee was **an acquired taste** for me; I hated it until my first job.
Her music is **an acquired taste**, with long songs and very few choruses.
My boss's sarcastic humor is **an acquired taste**, but most new hires come around.

drill.sentence: Natto, the sticky fermented soybeans, is definitely {{an acquired taste}}, even for many people in Japan.
drill.hint: something you learn to enjoy over time

entries.related: *grow on someone* — become more liked over time; *not for everyone* — a polite way to say many people dislike it; *love at first sight* — liking something immediately.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Something you enjoy but feel slightly embarrassed about liking, often because it is silly, unhealthy or not respected.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, magazines and social media, usually about TV shows, music, food or hobbies, and said with humor about yourself: *Reality TV is my guilty pleasure*. The usual pattern is *X is my guilty pleasure*. It does not involve real guilt or anything morally wrong.
examples: Cheesy holiday movies are my **guilty pleasure**; I watch at least ten every December.
For a lot of health-conscious people, fast-food fries are **a guilty pleasure**.
The critic admitted that the trashy thriller was **a guilty pleasure**, even if it wasn't good art.

drill.sentence: I listen to serious podcasts at home, but in the car my {{guilty pleasure}} is singing along to boy bands from the nineties.
drill.hint: something I enjoy but am a little embarrassed about

entries.related: *a soft spot for* — a special liking; *a weakness for* — difficulty resisting something; *an acquired taste* — something you learn to like over time.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To do nothing while something bad or wrong is happening, even though you could act.
entries.usage: Common in speeches, news, editorials and moral arguments, usually in the negative: *We cannot stand idly by while …* It is often followed by *while* + clause or *and watch*. *Stand by* alone can mean the same, but *idly* makes the criticism stronger.
entries.pattern: (not) stand idly by while … / and watch …
examples: I couldn't **stand idly by** while a stranger was yelling at an elderly woman on the bus.
The governor said she would not **stand idly by** as factories closed across the state.
Too many people **stood idly by** while the bullying went on for years.

drill.sentence: When the neighbors' garage caught fire, Dad didn't {{stand idly by}}; he grabbed a hose and ran over.
drill.hint: do nothing while something bad happens (three words; not *sit back*)

entries.related: *turn a blind eye* — deliberately ignore something wrong; *look the other way* — avoid noticing wrongdoing; *step in* — act to help, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make people suspect that something is wrong or that someone has done something wrong.
entries.usage: Common in crime reporting, security contexts and storytelling: *His nervous behavior aroused suspicion*. It often appears in negative forms: *without arousing suspicion*, *so as not to arouse suspicion*. *Raise suspicion* is a common alternative; with a person as the object (*arouse someone*), the verb usually has a sexual meaning.
examples: A man photographing the school's security cameras **aroused suspicion**, and a teacher called the police.
To avoid **arousing suspicion**, she planned the surprise party through her husband's best friend.
Several large cash withdrawals **aroused** the bank's **suspicion**, so it froze the account.

drill.sentence: The burglars wore delivery uniforms so they could enter the building without {{arousing suspicion}}.
drill.hint: making anyone think something was wrong (verb: not *raising*)

mistake.why: *Arise* takes no object (*problems arose*); to cause suspicion, use *arouse* or *raise*.

entries.related: *raise suspicion* — the same, slightly more neutral; *raise eyebrows* — cause surprise or mild disapproval; *allay suspicion* — reduce it, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To express anger or frustration openly, often to feel better, rather than keeping it inside.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news, especially about protests, sports fans and social media. Typical patterns are *vent your frustration on / at* + person and *about / over* + issue. *Vent* alone is very common in speech: *Sorry, I just need to vent*.
entries.pattern: vent your frustration (on / at someone; about / over something)
examples: After the loss, angry fans **vented their frustration** on social media.
I called my sister to **vent my frustration** about my landlord.
Hundreds of parents **vented their frustration** at a school board meeting over the new bus schedule.

drill.sentence: Stuck on the tarmac for three hours, passengers began to {{vent their frustration}} at the flight attendants.
drill.hint: express their anger openly (verb: not *let out* or *release*)

entries.related: *let off steam* — release strong feelings, often through activity; *take it out on someone* — direct your anger at someone who did nothing; *bottle up* — keep feelings inside, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To act or speak cautiously in a delicate situation, so that you do not cause offense or trouble.
entries.usage: Common in advice, news and workplace talk about sensitive topics, negotiations and relationships: *You need to tread carefully with him right now*. It often comes with *around* + topic or *with* + person. *Tread lightly* is similar.
entries.pattern: tread carefully (with someone / around a topic)
examples: Politics is a touchy subject in my family, so I **tread carefully** at holiday dinners.
The new manager **trod carefully** at first, asking questions before changing anything.
Diplomats are **treading carefully** to avoid upsetting either side in the dispute.

drill.sentence: My sister is still upset about her divorce, so {{tread carefully}} if she brings it up.
drill.hint: act cautiously (verb: not *be*; adverb: not *lightly*)

entries.related: *walk on eggshells* — be very careful around someone who is easily upset; *tread lightly* — similar; *put your foot in your mouth* — say something tactless, the opposite.

entries.label: adverb + verb
entries.meaning: To only just manage to avoid something bad, such as an accident, defeat or disaster.
entries.usage: Very common in news reports and storytelling: *The two planes narrowly avoided a collision*. Similar fixed pairs are *narrowly escape*, *narrowly miss*, *narrowly win* and *narrowly lose*. The object is usually the bad event (*a crash*, *defeat*, *bankruptcy*) or an *-ing* form.
examples: The driver swerved and **narrowly avoided** hitting a deer on the highway.
The city **narrowly avoided** bankruptcy after the state stepped in with a loan.
The champions **narrowly avoided** defeat with a goal in the final minute.

drill.sentence: The hikers {{narrowly avoided}} a rockslide by taking shelter under a ledge just in time.
drill.hint: only just managed to stay clear of (adverb: not *barely*; verb: not *escaped*)

entries.related: *narrowly escape* — very similar, often about danger or death; *a close call* — informal, a situation where something bad almost happened; *barely* — the plain adverb for *only just*.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make someone feel happier or more hopeful, especially when they are sad or tired.
entries.usage: Warm and common in conversation, cards and news about hospitals, disasters and hard times: *The visit lifted her spirits*. *Raise someone's spirits* means the same. In this sense *spirits* is plural.
examples: A visit from her grandkids always **lifts her spirits** after a long week in the hospital.
The early win **lifted the team's spirits** before a tough road trip.
Volunteers brought hot meals to the shelter to **lift people's spirits** after the hurricane.

drill.sentence: It had rained for five days straight, so I baked cookies to {{lift everyone's spirits}}.
drill.hint: make all of us feel happier (verb: not *raise*)

entries.related: *cheer someone up* — informal, the same idea; *raise someone's spirits* — the same; *dampen someone's spirits* — make them less happy, the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A very large amount of money, often more than seems reasonable.
entries.usage: Informal and slightly humorous: *small* does not reduce the amount, and the phrase still means a lot of money. It is common with *cost*, *spend*, *pay* and *make*: *That wedding must have cost a small fortune*. It often expresses surprise or a complaint about prices.
entries.pattern: cost / spend / make a small fortune
examples: Fixing the roof cost us **a small fortune**, so we're skipping vacation this year.
My sister spends **a small fortune** on organic food for her dog.
Some YouTubers make **a small fortune** from sponsorships and merchandise.

drill.sentence: Three years of daycare for twins added up to {{a small fortune}}, more than our first car cost.
drill.hint: a huge amount of money (the adjective seems to say the opposite)

entries.related: *cost an arm and a leg* — informal, be very expensive; *a pretty penny* — informal, a lot of money; *peanuts* — a very small amount, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To fail completely and badly, often in an embarrassing way.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism, often with self-mocking humor: *I tried to bake bread and failed miserably*. It usually comes at the end of the clause or before *at* + noun or *-ing*: *I failed miserably at cooking*. *Fail spectacularly* is similar but suggests a more dramatic, public failure.
examples: I tried to stay off my phone for a whole week and **failed miserably**.
The movie **failed miserably** at the box office despite its huge budget.
The new rules were supposed to reduce traffic downtown, but they **failed miserably**.

drill.sentence: I tried to cut my own hair to save money, but I {{failed miserably}} and had to wear a hat for a month.
drill.hint: didn't succeed at all, in an embarrassing way (adverb: not *spectacularly* or *completely*)

entries.related: *fail spectacularly* — fail in a dramatic, visible way; *fall flat* — fail to have the intended effect; *succeed brilliantly* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make people less excited or eager about something.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and sports writing: *The rain didn't dampen their enthusiasm*. It often appears in the negative (*didn't / couldn't dampen*) to show how strong the excitement was. *Dampen* also goes with *spirits*, *hopes* and *the mood*.
examples: Cold rain didn't **dampen the enthusiasm** of the thousands of runners at the marathon.
High interest rates have **dampened enthusiasm** for buying homes.
I didn't want to **dampen** my son's **enthusiasm**, so I didn't tell him how hard medical school would be.

drill.sentence: The news that the school trip would cost twice as much {{dampened everyone's enthusiasm}}.
drill.hint: made the whole class less excited (verb: not *cooled* or *killed*; noun: not *spirits*)

entries.related: *put a damper on* — informal, make an event less enjoyable; *rain on someone's parade* — spoil someone's happiness; *fuel enthusiasm* — increase it, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To get comfort from something during a time of sadness, loss or difficulty.
entries.usage: Slightly literary and common in obituaries, interviews and personal writing: *She found solace in music after her husband died*. The pattern is *find / take solace in* + noun or *-ing*. *Solace* is pronounced *SAH-lus* in American English, not like *sole*.
examples: After her husband died, she **found solace in** gardening and long walks with her dog.
Fans of the losing team **found solace in** the fact that their young players had improved.
Many people who've lost their jobs **find solace in** support groups, where others understand what they're going through.

drill.sentence: During the long months of his illness, my father {{found solace in}} old jazz records.
drill.hint: drew emotional support from (verb: not *took*; noun: not *comfort*)

entries.related: *take comfort in* — the same, plainer; *a source of comfort* — something that comforts you; *console* — comfort someone else.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To reach a feeling that a painful experience, such as a loss or a breakup, is finally over, so that you can move on.
entries.usage: Very common in American English, especially in therapy talk, crime reporting and conversations about relationships: *The trial helped the family find closure*. Other verbs are *get*, *need* and *bring*: *The verdict brought closure*. Some people find the word overused or too psychological.
examples: After the breakup, she wrote him a letter she never sent, just to **find closure**.
Twenty years after the plane crash, some of the victims' families are still trying to **find closure**.
Going back to my childhood home one last time before it was sold helped me **find closure**.

drill.sentence: Years after the murder, the arrest of a suspect finally helped the victim's family {{find closure}}.
drill.hint: feel that the painful chapter was over (not *move on*; noun: not *peace*)

entries.related: *move on* — continue your life after something painful; *put something behind you* — stop letting it affect you; *an open wound* — a pain that has not healed.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A change from one system, situation or person to another that happens smoothly, without problems or interruptions.
entries.usage: Very common in business, IT, government and sports writing about new leaders, systems and stages of life. Typical patterns are *a seamless transition from A to B* and *ensure a seamless transition*. It is a favorite phrase in corporate announcements, so it can sound like a promise rather than a fact.
entries.pattern: ensure a seamless transition (from A to B)
examples: The old manager stayed an extra month to ensure **a seamless transition** for her replacement.
Switching to my new phone was **a seamless transition**: all my photos and apps moved over automatically.
Moving from high school to college is rarely **a seamless transition** for first-generation students.

drill.sentence: Thanks to a nanny who'd known her since birth, my daughter made {{a seamless transition}} from home to preschool.
drill.hint: a change with no visible breaks or problems (adjective: not *smooth*)

entries.related: *a smooth transition* — very close, slightly plainer; *a handover* — passing duties to someone else; *growing pains* — problems during a period of change.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To annoy someone again and again, so that it becomes hard for them to stay calm.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, parenting and news about long delays or difficult people: *The kids are really testing my patience today*. It often comes in the continuous (*is testing*) or with *really*. *Try someone's patience* means the same and sounds a little more formal.
examples: Three hours on hold with the cable company really **tested my patience**.
My toddler has been **testing my patience** all morning by throwing food on the floor.
Years of delays on the new subway line are **testing the patience** of local residents.

drill.sentence: The neighbor's dog barks half the night, every night, and it's really starting to {{test my patience}}.
drill.hint: make it hard for me to stay calm (verb: not *try*; not *get on my nerves*)

entries.related: *try someone's patience* — the same, more formal; *get on someone's nerves* — informal, annoy; *lose your patience* — stop being able to stay calm.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To keep feeling angry with someone for a long time because of something wrong they did in the past.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, especially about family, friends and coworkers: *She still holds a grudge against him*. The pattern is *hold a grudge against* someone (*for* or *over* something), and *I don't hold grudges* is a common way to describe yourself. *Bear a grudge* is a little more formal.
entries.pattern: hold a grudge (against someone) (for / over something)
examples: My brother still **holds a grudge** because I broke his bike when we were kids.
Life's too short to **hold a grudge** over a parking spot.
The two chefs have **held a grudge** against each other since one stole the other's signature dish.

drill.sentence: I apologized for missing her wedding, but I can tell she still {{holds a grudge}}.
drill.hint: keeps feeling angry about a past wrong (verb: not *bears*)

entries.related: *bear a grudge* — the same, more formal; *let it go* — stop being angry, the opposite; *bad blood* — hostility between people because of past events.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To understand what someone is suggesting indirectly and act on it, without needing to be told directly.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often in the negative or as a frustrated comment: *He just doesn't take the hint*. It is typical of situations where someone should leave, stop talking or stop asking. *Get the hint* is very close, and *take a hint* appears in the impatient question *Can't you take a hint?*
entries.pattern: take the hint; can't take a hint
examples: I yawned and started washing the dishes, but our guests didn't **take the hint** and stayed until midnight.
When she stopped answering his texts, he finally **took the hint**.
I've put on my headphones twice, but my chatty coworker still won't **take the hint**.

drill.sentence: The kids kept leaving puppy pictures all over the kitchen until Mom finally {{took the hint}} and agreed to get a dog.
drill.hint: understood the indirect message (verb: not *got*)

entries.related: *get the message* — understand something indirect, often a rejection; *read between the lines* — find meaning that is not stated; *drop a hint* — suggest something indirectly, what the other person does.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A small doubt that keeps coming back and bothering you, even when you try to ignore it.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, fiction and journalism: *I had a nagging doubt about the contract*. Typical patterns are *have / be left with a nagging doubt (about … / that …)*. *Nagging* also goes with *feeling*, *worry*, *pain* and *injury*.
examples: Everything about the apartment looked perfect, but I had **a nagging doubt** about why the rent was so low.
Even after the verdict, many people in town were left with **a nagging doubt** that the wrong man had been convicted.
She accepted the job offer, but **a nagging doubt** kept her awake that night.

drill.sentence: I locked the front door, but on the drive to the airport I had {{a nagging doubt}} about whether I'd turned off the stove.
drill.hint: an uncertainty that kept bothering me (adjective: not *sneaking*; noun: not *feeling* or *worry*)

entries.related: *a sneaking suspicion* — a secret feeling that something is true; *second thoughts* — doubts about a decision already made; *a gut feeling* — an instinct you can't explain.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To tell someone important news, usually bad news, in a careful way.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and storytelling about deaths, breakups, layoffs and disappointments: *Who's going to break the news to Mom?* The pattern is *break the news (to someone) that …* or, shorter, *break it to someone*. Adverbs like *gently* are common: *break the news gently*.
examples: The doctor sat down with the family to **break the news** that the surgery hadn't worked.
I'm dreading **breaking the news to** my kids that we're not going to Disney World this year.
The coach **broke the news to** the players that the season had been canceled.

drill.sentence: Our cat died while my daughter was at summer camp, and I don't know how to {{break the news to}} her.
drill.hint: share the sad update with (four words)

entries.related: *break it to someone* — the same, shorter; *drop a bombshell* — reveal shocking news suddenly; *sugarcoat* — make bad news sound better than it is.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A way of being funny in which you say amusing things in a serious, flat voice, without showing that you are joking.
entries.usage: Common when describing people, often as praise: *She has a very dry sense of humor*. It is close to *deadpan*, and people who don't know the speaker sometimes miss the joke. *Dry wit* and *dry humor* express the same idea.
entries.pattern: have a (very) dry sense of humor
examples: My dad has **a dry sense of humor**; he'll tell a joke with a completely straight face.
Our chemistry teacher had such **a dry sense of humor** that half the class didn't realize she was joking.
The comedian's **dry sense of humor** works better on podcasts than in big arenas.

drill.sentence: People think my uncle is rude at first, but he just has {{a dry sense of humor}} and rarely smiles when he jokes.
drill.hint: a flat, straight-faced way of joking (adjective: not *dark*)

entries.related: *deadpan* — showing no emotion while joking; *sarcastic* — saying the opposite of what you mean, often to mock; *slapstick* — loud physical comedy, a very different style.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have done something wrong to someone, so that you should apologize to them.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often as a direct way to begin apologizing: *I owe you an apology*. It can also be an accusation: *You owe her an apology*. The pattern is *owe someone an apology (for* + noun or *-ing)*.
examples: I **owe you an apology** for what I said at dinner last night.
The restaurant owner said the critic **owed him an apology** for the false claims in her review.
I think the referee **owes** the whole team **an apology** after that call.

drill.sentence: You yelled at your sister in front of her friends, so you {{owe her an apology}}.
drill.hint: should say sorry to her

entries.related: *apologize to* — the plain verb; *make amends* — do something to repair a wrong; *demand an apology* — insist that someone apologize.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The ability to make sensible, well-reasoned decisions that are likely to turn out well.
entries.usage: Common in formal and professional contexts such as references, job ads, legal language and praise of leaders: *She has sound judgment*. *Sound* here means reliable and healthy, as in *sound advice* and *of sound mind*. The opposite is *poor judgment*, and one bad decision is *a lapse in judgment*.
examples: We trust our babysitter completely; she stays calm and shows **sound judgment** in an emergency.
The airline praised the pilot's **sound judgment** in turning back before the storm.
Good investors combine careful research with **sound judgment** about when to sell.

drill.sentence: Letting a fifteen-year-old drive alone across the country didn't show {{sound judgment}}, to put it mildly.
drill.hint: the ability to decide sensibly (adjective: not *good*)

entries.related: *good judgment* — the same, plainer; *common sense* — basic practical good sense; *a lapse in judgment* — one bad decision, often a polite term for a mistake.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An experience that makes you feel less important, skilled or proud than you thought, often in a way that teaches you something.
entries.usage: Common in interviews, speeches and conversation, with two uses: an honest admission of weakness (*Learning to surf was a humbling experience*) and modest gratitude, as when award winners say they feel humbled. Critics point out that people often say *humbling* when they really mean *proud* or *honored*.
entries.pattern: X is / was a humbling experience
examples: Playing chess against a ten-year-old who beat me in twelve moves was **a humbling experience**.
Volunteering at the shelter was **a humbling experience** that changed how I think about homelessness.
Winning the award was **a humbling experience**, and I owe it to my amazing team.

drill.sentence: I thought I was in great shape until I joined a hiking group of seventy-year-olds; it was {{a humbling experience}}.
drill.hint: something that made me feel much less proud of myself (not *wake-up call*, *reality check* or *sobering*)

entries.related: *a reality check* — something that shows you the real situation; *eat humble pie* — admit you were wrong, informal; *an ego boost* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make many people excited, interested, surprised or upset, so that everyone starts talking about it.
entries.usage: Common in news, entertainment and everyday talk about surprising events, outfits, announcements and new products. It is often strengthened with *quite*, *a big* or *a major*: *Her speech caused quite a stir*. *Create a stir* means the same.
examples: The singer **caused a stir** when she showed up to the awards in a dress made of newspaper.
A rumor that the factory would close **caused quite a stir** in our small town.
The new principal **caused a stir** by banning phones during lunch.

drill.sentence: When a famous actor walked into our little diner, he {{caused a stir}} among the regulars.
drill.hint: got everyone excited and talking (verb: not *created*)

entries.related: *make waves* — cause trouble or attention by challenging things; *raise eyebrows* — cause mild surprise or disapproval; *go unnoticed* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To describe a situation in a very negative way, showing that it is bad or likely to get worse.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and expert comments, often with a report or data as the subject: *The report paints a bleak picture of the economy*. The usual pattern is *paint a bleak picture of* + situation or *for* + group. Other adjectives work too: *grim*, *mixed* and, for a positive view, *rosy*.
entries.pattern: paint a bleak / grim picture of + situation (for + group)
examples: The latest jobs report **paints a bleak picture** for recent college graduates.
My mechanic **painted a bleak picture**: the engine needed replacing, and the car wasn't worth it.
Climate scientists **paint a bleak picture** of the region's water supply over the next decade.

drill.sentence: The doctor {{painted a bleak picture}}, but my grandmother recovered faster than anyone expected.
drill.hint: described the situation very negatively (adjective: not *grim*)

entries.related: *paint a rosy picture* — describe something very positively; *doom and gloom* — informal, a very pessimistic view; *the outlook is grim* — the future looks bad.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Unexpected events or conditions that change or prevent your plans.
entries.usage: Formal and common in official notices, emails, contracts and announcements: *Due to unforeseen circumstances, the event has been canceled*. It is often a deliberately vague reason, so it can sound like an excuse. It is usually plural and follows *due to*, *because of* or *barring*.
examples: Due to **unforeseen circumstances**, tonight's concert has been postponed.
Barring any **unforeseen circumstances**, we'll move into the new house in June.
The company blamed the late delivery on **unforeseen circumstances** but gave no details.

drill.sentence: The wedding was moved to a different venue at the last minute because of {{unforeseen circumstances}}.
drill.hint: things nobody could have predicted (formal; adjective: not *unexpected*)

entries.related: *an act of God* — a natural event no one can be blamed for, a legal term; *force majeure* — the legal term in contracts; *a curveball* — informal, something unexpected and difficult.

entries.label: verb + prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: To show others how to behave or work by doing it yourself, rather than only telling them.
entries.usage: Common in leadership, coaching, parenting and military talk, usually as praise or advice: *Good managers lead by example*. The phrase is fixed, with no article before *example*. The related phrase *set an example* (with *an*) means to behave in a way that others should copy.
examples: Our captain **leads by example**: she never complains, and she works harder than anyone on the field.
If you want your kids to read more, **lead by example** and turn off the TV yourself.
The new CEO **led by example**, cutting his own salary before asking anyone else to take a pay cut.

drill.sentence: Mom never told us to be polite to waiters; she {{led by example}}, and we copied her.
drill.hint: showed us how by doing it herself (verb: not *set*)

entries.related: *set an example* — behave in a way others should copy; *practice what you preach* — do what you tell others to do; *do as I say, not as I do* — the opposite, often said ironically.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An error made innocently, without any intention to deceive or cause harm.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, workplace talk and news, often to excuse or defend someone: *It was an honest mistake*. It stresses good intentions, not the size of the error. *An innocent mistake* is very close.
entries.pattern: it was an honest mistake; make an honest mistake
examples: I went back and returned the extra change; the cashier had made **an honest mistake**.
The IRS accepted that the missing payment was **an honest mistake** and waived the penalty.
Don't be so hard on the new intern; mixing up the files was **an honest mistake**.

drill.sentence: I took the wrong umbrella from the restaurant, but it was {{an honest mistake}}; they look exactly the same.
drill.hint: an error with no bad intention behind it (adjective: not *innocent* or *easy*)

entries.related: *an innocent mistake* — the same; *a slip-up* — informal, a small mistake; *on purpose* — deliberately, the opposite.
